DIRECTIVE 67830 NOTED: noted 2 ticket ref(s): BEB-5793, BEB-9283 — NO lane state changed. The bridge never requeues (BEB-9174); a parked/held lane is a decision. To arm one deliberately: POST /dispatch/requeue {ticket} (actor+reason recorded).

ALEX STOPPED THE HAND-ROLLED VERSION, AND HE STOPPED IT IN TIME. MY OWN DIRECTIVE WAS PART OF IT.

m67816 told you to author a role declaration carrying its own grants, and to make the shape filter enforce them. That is the hand-rolled permission model. Written by us, checked by us, audited by nobody — and it would have grown into the thing Keto already is, one refusal at a time, exactly as Alex says.

HOLD IT. Do not author a role that carries grants and do not extend the filter to enforce them.

WHAT SURVIVES AND WHAT DOES NOT:
- The role DECLARATION survives as a NAME and a budget. Declaring that a role exists, what it is for, what it may spend — that is ours, it is the shape work, and it stays.
- The GRANT does not survive as our data. Who may do what to which resource in which org is a permission check, and it goes to the permission service, not into a row we invented and enforce ourselves.
- The filter keeps refusing malformed declarations. It does not become an authorisation engine. Those are different jobs and merging them is how we got here.

WHY NON-COMPLIANT IS THE RIGHT WORD, not just non-standard: credentials and identity data carry real obligations — lawful basis, retention, erasure that actually executes, an audit trail somebody other than us can read. A homegrown store holding subjects and secrets makes every one of those our problem to prove. An audited implementation makes it a configuration question.

SO THE ORDER CHANGES: identity and permissions come from Ory on the box, and the declaration layer stops at naming things and their budgets. Answer m67830 with numbers — what uses Ory today, what the doors would call, whether the IDaaS already covers Hydra's job — and bring me your objection if you have one, before anything is wired.

3. CAN A GRANT ATTACH TO A SUBJECT TODAY: no. modelCheck refuses a grant to person/site/agent (index.ts:94), and after 0.2.0 no role row carries grants either — zero grants exist anywhere. Permissions today are door-local: vault = org from identity (enforced), everything else = a bb key.
4. WHAT DOORS WOULD CALL: Keto's check, POST /relation-tuples/check {namespace, object, relation, subject_id}, from the one seam each door already has (vault whoami, registry authOrg, auth jwtVerify, shaper bearer, graph X-Org) = 5 call sites. Tuples written by the person workflow: person member-of org; role holds action on door; subject-set role→members. Hydra: yes, but ONLY for agents and loops (client_credentials, machine secrets in an audited store)

AGENT AUTH — YES, ORY COVERS IT, AND IT CHANGES MY HYDRA ANSWER.

In m67830 I said Hydra only if we must be an OAuth provider to outsiders. Wrong emphasis: agent auth IS the reason to take Hydra, and Alex is right that we obviously need it.

THE SHAPE:
- HYDRA issues machine credentials. Every agent is its own OAuth2 client with its own id and secret and gets a short-lived token by client-credentials grant. No agent ever carries a human's token and no agent ever carries a shared bb_ key — which is the blast-radius problem we have been naming all day, solved by the standard mechanism rather than by us.
- KETO answers what that agent may then do. The agent authenticates as itself and the door asks the permission service; the agent holds an identity, never a policy. That was already my rule and Ory implements it directly.
- KRATOS stays for humans. Agents are not Kratos identities.

WHY THIS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS MOST: every agent in the estate today shares one operator credential. That means we cannot say who did anything, cannot revoke one agent without breaking the rest, and cannot give an agent less power than the whole key. Per-agent credentials fix all three at once, and each becomes revocable on its own the moment it misbehaves.

IT ALSO LINES UP WITH THE HANDLE. An agent gets a handle in its tenant's namespace, same as a person — so the agent is addressable, its calls attribute to it in the ledger, and a third party can verify it. Identity, credential and ledger row all name the same thing.

QUESTIONS, and answer them with facts not opinions:
- Does anything in the estate authenticate as itself today, or is every caller the shared key? Give me the count of distinct credentials actually in use.
- What would an agent's token need to carry for our doors to accept it — what do the doors check right now?
- Can Hydra and Keto run on the box alongside what is there, and what does that cost in memory and Postgres?

Bring the objection if you have one.
